title: Education as foundation for sustainable development
seoTitle: Education as foundation for sustainable development
subtitle: How strengthening learning can transform vulnerable economies and ensure a greener future
excerpt: Education is the engine that drives sustainability in developing countries, providing tools to tackle environmental and social challenges in an integrated way.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
Amid growing climate crises and socioeconomic inequalities, education emerges as the most decisive element for developing countries to achieve truly sustainable growth. Without investment in quality learning, clean energy initiatives, natural resource management, and social inclusion tend to fail, perpetuating cycles of poverty and environmental degradation.

Global context

In recent decades, international bodies such as the UN and the World Bank have solidified the idea that sustainable development cannot be separated from education. The 2030 Agenda, for example, includes Quality Education (Goal 4) as a prerequisite for climate action (Goal 13) and poverty eradication (Goal 1). While most high-income countries have already progressed in literacy and school enrollment indicators, many emerging nations still face illiteracy rates that exceed the global average.

Why education influences sustainability

The link between learning and sustainability operates in three dimensions. First, awareness: informed citizens recognize the impacts of their consumption choices and demand stricter environmental policies. Second, technical capacity: schools and universities that incorporate environmental sciences, agroecology, and renewable energy train professionals capable of implementing innovative solutions. Finally, social inclusion: education reduces gender and income disparities, enabling historically marginalized groups to actively participate in preservation and resource management projects.

Challenges faced by developing countries

Even while recognizing its value, many nations still stumble over structural obstacles. The scarcity of financial resources often limits the construction of adequate school infrastructures, while the lack of qualified teachers hinders the inclusion of sustainability content in curricula. Moreover, rural areas frequently lack internet access, making it difficult to adopt distance-learning methodologies that could broaden the reach of good practices. These barriers create a vicious circle: low educational outcomes generate reduced innovation capacity, which in turn diminishes economic competitiveness and maintains dependence on resource-intensive sectors.

What Brazil can learn

For the Brazilian reader, the national experience offers valuable lessons. Programs such as Fundeb demonstrate that continuous investment in school funding can raise enrollment rates and improve teaching quality. Likewise, regional agroecology initiatives in Northeast schools show how integrating local knowledge with modern science can produce healthier food and reduce pressure on ecosystems. Observing these cases makes it clear that public policies aligning financial resources, teacher training, and curricular content are essential for education to effectively contribute to sustainability.

Outlook and recommendations

To transform education into a driver of sustainable development, experts point to four priority lines of action:

  • Stable and targeted funding: ensure long-term budgetary resources for the construction and maintenance of schools, as well as for the acquisition of environmental teaching materials.
  • Ongoing teacher training: create capacity-building programs that include sustainability teaching methodologies, use of digital technologies, and project-based learning practices.
  • Integrated curricula: embed transversal competencies – such as critical thinking, problem solving, and ecological citizenship – across all subjects, from primary to higher education.
  • Multi-sectoral partnerships: encourage collaboration among governments, universities, NGOs, and the private sector to develop innovation labs, internships, and community projects that put classroom-acquired knowledge into practice.

These measures, when adapted to each country's reality, enhance the ability to generate local solutions that meet global sustainability goals.

Conclusion

In summary, education is not only a fundamental right, but the strategic element that enables developing countries to overcome environmental and social challenges simultaneously. By investing in quality learning, these nations create a virtuous cycle of knowledge, innovation, and inclusion that benefits both natural resource preservation and economic growth. For Brazil, observing and adapting international best practices can accelerate the transition to a more resilient and equitable development model, reinforcing the nation's role as a protagonist in the global sustainability agenda.
